messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The night Darius was attacked in the underpass still surfaces not as a narrative but as fractured frames he cannot piece together. He remembers the heavy thud of a bottle striking brick, the sudden flash of a man’s face twisting into rage, and the sharp, sour reek of cheap whiskey on the attacker’s breath. When the memory returns, the emotion is so overwhelming that he is forced to stop everything he is doing, and he knows he cannot find the words to describe what happened. These intrusive, wordless snapshots quickly hijack his present life; the mere sight of someone gesturing emphatically, even a colleague explaining a zoning map in a measured tone, or the whiff of alcohol in a crowded transit car, directly fuels his constant state of alarm. His body jumps at ordinary sounds, and unexpected movement nearby causes him to react as if he is in immediate danger. Because he cannot trust safety, even when others tell him he is fine, the world feels perpetually hostile. The fragmented, wordless nature of his recall directly feeds into his negative appraisals, convincing him that the institutions meant to protect him failed him completely, that he is fundamentally ill-equipped to handle stress, and that he is powerless against bad outcomes. Those interpretations quickly dictate his daily survival habits. Believing he cannot cope with the slightest upset, Darius avoids conflict in every possible setting, muting his own professional opinions to keep the peace. His conviction that bad things are inevitable also pushes him toward gambling, which he uses to distract himself and manufacture a fleeting sense of excitement. The memory of the assault directly fuels these maladaptive strategies; because the event returns as overwhelming, wordless pictures, he has no psychological bandwidth for healthy regulation, so he retreats into betting and silence. Conversely, his avoidance and numbing tactics actively worsen his internal state. By sidestepping disagreement, he reinforces his belief that he is fundamentally incompetent, which in turn sharpens his threat monitoring. Every time he places a bet to escape his feelings, the temporary relief fades, leaving his startle reflex more wound and his nervous system primed to interpret ordinary sounds or sudden movements as fresh attacks. These new threat spikes then trigger the original sensory cues again, pulling the traumatic snapshots forward with renewed intensity. The cycle tightens with each passing month: his coping rituals deepen his helplessness, his helplessness amplifies his hyperarousal, and his hyperarousal makes every trigger feel lethal. The sheer physiological toll of these interactions has left him chronically exhausted, a reality his supervisors notice but misunderstand as simple burnout. Working as an urban planner in downtown Chicago has become a daily exercise in navigating these hidden fault lines. During a recent site walk with a development team, a contractor raised his voice while pointing out a drainage discrepancy. The sound alone triggered a full-body flinch that made Darius drop his clipboard. Instead of addressing the misunderstanding, he abruptly excused himself, claiming a prior commitment, and retreated to his car where he spent the next hour placing rapid, escalating bets on a mobile app. The distraction worked temporarily, but it left him paralyzed when returning to the office, convinced he had irreparably damaged his professional credibility. The longer he maintained this pattern of retreat and numbing, the more he believed he could never prevent future disasters, and the more his mind sharpened its radar for the very signs of violence he desperately wanted to avoid. What finally drove him to seek therapy was a Tuesday morning when a simple spilled coffee at his desk triggered a panic attack so severe he feared he would lose his job. He came to the clinic hoping to stop the cycle, terrified that without intervention, he would remain trapped in a vigilance he could neither control nor escape.
